case_study_insert.main_stem: Kettlewell Furniture (KWF) is a cooperative in the flat-pack and upholstered furniture retail sector, employing a workforce of 58 across its Brandleford workshop, showroom and delivery team. Founded in 2004 by Margaret Ellison, the member-owned cooperative operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. KWF plans to invest $640,000 in a large Brandleford showroom with a click-and-collect warehouse, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $34, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. KWF faces a growing operational problem: material waste in the cutting workshop has risen to 9.4% and damaged-stock write-offs are increasing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — October 2026: The Brandleford cutting workshop processed 640 sofa frames last quarter; material waste fell from 9.4% to 7.1% after nesting software was introduced. Showroom complaints about damaged deliveries fell from 27 to 15 per month. The assembly defect rate is 4.7%. A survey of 520 co-op members found 66% prefer locally made furniture and 41% would pay 8% more for it. Average delivery time is 6 days. Off-the-job training at the Brandleford college costs $850 per employee, while on-the-job training is supervised by workshop mentors.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 5.0% in two 0.5% rises this year, increasing costs for borrowers with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 8.0% from $11.20 to $12.10 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for hourly-paid workshop and showroom staff. (3) Timber, foam and fabric input costs rose 14.6% year-on-year, inflation is running at 4.2%, and furniture retail spending grew only 1.3% in the same period.

questions.question_text: KWF plans to finance its $640,000 Brandleford showroom with a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for KWF of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs KWF no interest or arrangement fees, which matters because the cooperative already carries a 4.7% assembly defect rate and must fund waste-cutting work in the cutting workshop. KWF's control of its own cash becomes more precious now that the central bank has lifted the base rate to 5.0%: a variable-rate $400,000 loan already costs $2,000 a year for each 0.5% rise (0.005 x $400,000), so the 1.0% rise this year adds $4,000 a year, and borrowing any more would deepen that burden.

Point 2: Internal funding keeps the cooperative's member ownership undiluted and avoids lender covenants that could restrict showroom merchandising, pricing or member benefits. It also preserves KWF's standing with its 520 surveyed members, 66% of whom prefer locally made furniture: demonstrating that the $640,000 expansion is funded without overstretching debt reassures members, supports the membership drive behind the showroom, and protects the $34 price point while furniture spending grows only 1.3% and input costs inflate 14.6%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Kettlewell Furniture and its showroom expansion.

questions.question_text: KWF is opening its Brandleford showroom. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media marketing. Which should KWF choose to promote the opening? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would deliver massive brand reach and could showcase KWF's upholstered furniture to a national audience in seconds, dramatising the local-made story at scale. For a single Brandleford showroom whose delivery range covers only the surrounding region, however, the wastage of national airtime is enormous, and the production and slot costs would dwarf KWF's $240,000 retained-profit contribution to the $640,000 budget at a time when input costs are rising 14.6%.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is affordable, trusted and geographically precise for the Brandleford catchment, and sponsoring home and garden or weekend shows fits KWF's local-made story told to the 66% of members who prefer it. Its reach is limited to listeners, it lacks visual impact for furniture buyers, and younger purchasers increasingly ignore radio entirely, so attendance at the opening would depend on repeat slots and promotions rather than a single broadcast.

Social media marketing: Social media lets KWF show sofa-building reels, before-and-after cutting-workshop clips, and member testimonials, targeting exactly the 41% of members who would pay 8% more for locally made furniture. It is measurable, interactive and cheap, drives showroom footfall and click-and-collect pre-orders, and suits a flat-organisation founder brand like Margaret Ellison's; it does require consistent creative effort and at least a modest paid boost around launch week.

Recommendation: KWF should choose social media marketing. It aligns with KWF's member research, costs far less than television, reaches beyond radio's listener base with story-led owned media, and is measurable against showroom footfall and the 30,000-unit production plan. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for one regional showroom; local radio is rejected as audio-only with weaker appeal to younger buyers, so it should only support the launch as a short sponsorship burst rather than lead the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KWF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KWF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KWF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: KWF faces rising material waste and a 4.7% assembly defect rate. Explain two advantages for KWF of its autocratic leadership style when cutting workshop waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Margaret Ellison and workshop supervisors issue non-negotiable waste-cutting standards, nesting software settings, offcut reuse routines and inspection checkpoints, and enforce them immediately. In a cutting workshop where 640 frames were processed last quarter, quick, uniform decisions matter; a slow consultative process would let waste creep back above the improved 7.1% achieved after nesting software was introduced.

Point 2: Clear top-down accountability makes it obvious who owns each quality outcome, the cut, the assembly bench and the dispatch bay, so defective frames are caught before delivery rather than after. This directly attacks the 4.7% assembly defect rate and the complaint count about damaged deliveries, which has already fallen from 27 to 15 per month. The flat structure means supervisors sit close to the work, and autocratic clarity suits safety-critical cutting-machinery rules; KWF should pair directives with briefings so all 58 employees understand the reasons, or motivation and the co-op culture may suffer.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of autocratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KWF's waste, defects and flat structure.

questions.question_text: KWF wants to reduce the 4.7% assembly defect rate and waste above 7.1%. Consider on-the-job training in the workshop or off-the-job training at the Brandleford college. Which should KWF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Workshop-mentored training fits KWF's nesting software, machine settings and frame designs exactly, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 58 employees productive while standards are tightened. It is ideal for correcting the habits behind the 4.7% assembly defect rate, measuring, doweling, gluing and final checks, and it builds directly on the waste improvement from 9.4% to 7.1%. Risks include inconsistent coaching quality between mentors and busier mentors making errors under pressure.

Off-the-job training: The Brandleford college at $850 per employee gives structured health-and-safety, quality-systems and machine-care content with certificates, raising the workshop's professional standing. Training the whole workforce would cost $49,300 (58 x $850), well within reach but a heavy sum for a single site, and college training removes staff from productive cutting and assembly time, worsening the 6-day average delivery time precisely when the showroom build is underway. The content is generic, so KWF's exact frame designs still need practising in-house afterwards.

Decision: KWF should choose on-the-job training, led by its strongest assembly mentors, with the college reserved for one or two quality champions. It is immediate, specific to the workshop's machinery and free of fees, and protects the 6-day delivery promise while waste falls further from the 7.1% level. Full off-the-job training is rejected because $49,300 plus absence cover would strain the $264,000 fixed-cost base during the showroom build, and generic content would need customising to KWF's frames anyway; mentor-led coaching keeps every upholsterer aligned with the 4.7% defect target without losing a single shift of cutting output.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KWF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of KWF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of KWF with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and workshop relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KWF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $264,000 / ($34 - $22) = $264,000 / $12 = 22,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 22,000 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Current output - Break-even output. Substitution: 30,000 units - 22,000 units = 8,000 units. Answer: the margin of safety is 8,000 units.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KWF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. KWF can weigh the 22,000-unit break-even output against its 30,000-unit output, giving a margin of safety of 8,000 units (26.7% of output), and check whether member demand justifies adding showroom capacity next year.
2. The $12 contribution per unit lets managers model the effect of input-cost inflation; an extra $3.21 per unit (14.6% x $22) would cut contribution to $8.79, forcing a showroom pricing review before further promotional discounting.
3. Break-even analysis helps KWF time loan repayments on the $400,000 bank loan; with 22,000 units needed to cover $264,000 of fixed costs, each further 1,000 units adds $12,000 of contribution, so managers can schedule hires and refurbishment phases without slipping below break-even.
4. Managers can track unit cost ($264,000 / 30,000 units + $22 = $30.80 per unit) quarter by quarter, linking it to waste (9.4% falling to 7.1%) and the 4.7% defect rate to identify whether workshop savings or supplier renegotiation will drive the bigger gain before the showroom opens.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 22,000 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 8,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: safety headroom vs 30,000-unit output; input-cost stress test on the $12 contribution; $400,000 loan phasing against break-even; and unit-cost tracking at $30.80 to target waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KWF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KWF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.22 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.38 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.52 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.59 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $365,000; 2025 current assets = $260,000 + $110,000 + $85,000 = $455,000. Ratio 2024 = $365,000 / $300,000 = 1.22; 2025 = $455,000 / $330,000 = 1.38. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($365,000 - $210,000) / $300,000 = $155,000 / $300,000 = 0.52; 2025 = ($455,000 - $260,000) / $330,000 = $195,000 / $330,000 = 0.59.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved, but only modestly. The coverage of current assets over current liabilities rose from 1.22 to 1.38, and the quick measure excluding inventories rose from 0.52 to 0.59; cash improved from $60,000 to $85,000 and receivables from $95,000 to $110,000, while inventories climbed from $210,000 to $260,000 ahead of the $640,000 showroom opening. The heavy stock build is the main drag on the quick measure, and with furniture retail spending growing only 1.3% there is a real risk the extra stock moves slowly; inventories convert to cash only when the showroom and click-and-collect channels start selling.

Conclusion: KWF's financial position has improved, but the improvement is modest and inventory-led. The current ratio (1.22 to 1.38) and the acid test ratio (0.52 to 0.59) show stronger short-term cover, yet both years remain tighter than is comfortable for a cooperative about to carry $640,000 of new obligations. KWF should keep the nesting-software waste gains, tighten receivables from trade buyers and avoid loading stock beyond member demand before the showroom proves itself.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether KWF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KWF of selling locally made furniture at an 8% premium to members.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: 41% of surveyed co-op members would pay 8% more for locally made furniture and 66% prefer it, so the premium aligns margin with genuine member values rather than wishful pricing. Lifting the $34 price point by 8% on qualifying member lines would add roughly $2.72 per unit before any cost change, defending KWF against the 14.6% timber and foam input-cost rise, generating surplus to fund the $640,000 showroom, and differentiating KWF from imported flat-pack competitors on authenticity and local provenance.

Disadvantage: An 8% premium narrows the audience to high-commitment members and could deter the silent majority of walk-in showroom customers, especially while furniture spending is growing only 1.3%. If the premium spreads beyond the lines members specifically asked for, KWF risks weaker traffic, steeper discounting later, more unsold stock on top of the $260,000 inventory balance, and strain on the showroom business case; the premium also depends on members trusting the local-made claim, so KWF must keep the 7.1% waste and 4.7% defect gains visible to justify paying more.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KWF's member research, input costs and showroom plan.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 8.0% minimum wage increase and the 14.6% rise in input costs will affect KWF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 5.0%): If KWF's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, each 0.5% rise costs 0.005 x $400,000 = $2,000 a year, so the full 1.0% rise adds $4,000 a year (0.01 x $400,000). That is roughly 1.5% of fixed costs and is affordable, although it raises the hurdle on any further borrowing after the showroom opens and reduces the cash available to fund member dividends and refit phases.

Minimum wage increase (8.0%, to $12.10 per hour): KWF's workshop, showroom and delivery teams include hourly-paid workers, so the rise applies widely and is compulsory from April 2026. Hours and pay rates are not stated in the insert, so no exact annual total can be invented; against productivity of 30,000 units / 58 employees = 517.2 units per employee, the rise is absorbable only if output grows and the 7.1% waste gains hold, otherwise the $22 variable cost rises in effect and the $12 contribution per unit squeezes.

Input cost inflation (14.6% timber, foam and fabric): As an explicit upper bound, if the full $22 variable cost rose with input inflation it would add $3.21 per unit (0.146 x $22); at 30,000 units a year that is about $96,300 a year. Even partial pass-through halves the $12 contribution, and with furniture spending growing only 1.3% KWF cannot simply reprice the whole range; the 8% premium strategy adopted by the 41% of members who would pay more covers only part of the mix. Higher inputs also worsen the damaged-stock write-off until workshop savings catch up.

Conclusion: The 14.6% input cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across every unit KWF produces, is largely outside KWF's control, and lands precisely when demand growth is weakest at 1.3%. The interest rise caps at $4,000 a year and the wage rise is bounded by productivity gains from nesting software, so input costs threaten the $12 contribution that justifies the entire $640,000 showroom. KWF should lock in supplier contracts, extend the waste programme, and lean into the 8% local premium to protect margin.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KWF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KWF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KWF with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
